adjudication.reason: B identifies adolescent rye bread as the intended whole-grain exposure, but its estimate combines prevalent and incident diagnoses. The article reports the corresponding incident-only adjusted OR of 0.82 (95% CI 0.56–1.20). Exact analytical N for that sensitivity estimate is unavailable; the full early-life sample N must not be substituted. Unverified optional cases was omitted; no unsupported value is saved.

evidence.quote: Among the 347 prostate cancer cases who reported their dietary habits, 214 were diagnosed before and 133 after completing the FFQ.

In a sensitivity analysis we used logistic regression models to calculate ORs and 95% CIs of prostate cancer for rye- and oatmeal consumption in early life for incident cases only, adjusting for the same covariates as was done in the third model.

Compared with men consuming rye bread less than once per day, the OR in the multivariate model for total prostate cancer was 0.82 (95% CI: 0.56-1.20) and 0.73 (95% CI: 0.32-1.68) for advanced disease among men with high rye bread consumption in adolescence.
We compared men who were high (daily or more) and low (less than daily) consumers of rye bread in early life and midlife.

evidence.quote: Our final analytic cohort consisted of 288,268 men.
During an average of 9 years of follow-up, a total of 23,281 incident prostate cancer cases were ascertained.
Hazard ratios (HR) and 95% confidence intervals (CI) for associations with prostate cancer were estimated using Cox proportional hazards models, with person-years as the time variable.
Intakes of fat and fatty acids were categorized into quintiles and entered into models as nominal variables with the lowest category as the reference group.
There was a suggestive trend of decreased risk of fatal prostate cancer with increasing intake of EPA (highest vs. lowest quintile HR 0.82; 95% CI 0.64–1.04; p-for-trend 0.02).
Total prostate cancer cases included all men diagnosed with first primary prostate cancer of any grade.
